E1873.summary: Vaughan's term, as quoted, for the working strength of the finished Stone, which casting it on gold serves to qualify.
E1873.body: A term in a passage Atwood quotes from Vaughan: the Stone, once made, is cast on gold “to qualify the utensive power of it when it was made” [IV.3 ¶22]. The context suggests it means the medicine's working strength, which this bodily fermentation tempers.

E1874.summary: Named a worthy disciple of Paracelsus; Atwood cites him often as eyewitness of the Stone and on the labour, the Hand, the operator and the physician.
E1874.body:
Named with Crollius, Fludd, Helvetius and Faber among the intelligent, worthy disciples of Paracelsus [I.1 ¶64].

**Witness of the Stone.** From his *Book of Eternal Life* and *Ortus Med.*, Atwood cites his eyewitness account of projection on quicksilver yielding gold, with powder received from the stranger Butler: “I have seen the Stone and handled it” [I.1 ¶76; I.1 n98]. She also reports his cures of some 10,000 people yearly without diminishing his medicine [IV.3 ¶35].

**On the work.** From the *Oreatrike* she takes that “the attainment of the Tree of Life is laborious, and the fruit of intellectual research” [III.1 ¶13; III.1 n13]; the white sand Quellum in a vital soil never pierced [III.2 ¶8; III.2 n9]; another favoured individual led to perceive the simple element of nature — “I saw, as in a dream, the whole face of the earth” [III.2 ¶17; III.2 n18]; the requirements of the operator and the specific, not corrosive, dissolving virtue — “Not every messenger, says Van helmont, approacheth to the mine of Sontes” [IV.1 ¶39; IV.1 n30]; and the Hand as the soul's instrument, “The Hand, says Van Helmont, is the instrument of instruments”, with learners bidden to buy coals and fire and labour as philosophers did [IV.1 ¶5; IV.1 ¶7; IV.1 n3; IV.1 n9]. *Imago Mentis* and *Tree of Life* are cited for the three principles into which Life is resolved, “Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury” [III.2 ¶28; III.2 n27].

**On medicine.** From *Tumulus Pestis* she cites the requirements of the God-chosen physician (“But a physician chosen by God”) and medicine's decline through ambition and gain, calling him “one of its brightest ornaments” [IV.3 ¶34; IV.3 ¶35; IV.3 n12; IV.3 n13].

**Qualifications.** With Paracelsus he corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea (“by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit”), but Atwood treats this as only a secondary witness [III.3 n27]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer) he is said to speak of the White Light as the Quellem “in a very superficial way” [APP ¶157].

forms: the Van Helmonts, father and son
E1875.summary: The Van Helmonts, father and son, listed by Atwood among the adepts, with de Ortu Medicinae and Paradoxes cited.
E1875.body: Listed among the adepts, with *de Ortu Medicinae* and *Paradoxes* cited in the note [I.1 ¶70; I.1 n82].

E1876.summary: The material principle in conception, which obscures the generative light to bring it into sense and must be wholly evaporated before truth appears.
E1876.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood says: “The vaporous vehicle is the material principle in the conception” [APP ¶121]. It obscures the paternal generative light so as to bring it into sense, and “The whole of the self-included vaporous vehicle of the soul must be evaporated before any truth is evolved.” [APP ¶121]

E1877.summary: Thomas Vaughan, 'an English Adept', a much-cited modern authority on the First Matter, the Light, the fire, the furnace and the operator's discipline.
E1877.body:
**Who, per the book.** Thomas Vaughan translated and commented on the Rosicrucian *Fame and Confession*, with preface and appendix, and is sometimes confused with Philalethes [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶73]. Atwood praises him as showing the Art of vital perfectibility most clearly of English authors, gives his pseudonym Eugenius Philalethes, lists his works (*Magia Adamica*, *Coelum Terrae*, *Anthroposophia Theomagica*, *Anima Magia Abscondita*, *Euphrates*, *Lumen de Lumine*) and reports his death by overdose of the elixir [I.1 ¶74]. She calls him “an English Adept, neither antique nor envious” [III.4 ¶44]; “So wrote Vaughan in 1650” [III.1 ¶9].

**Matter and Light.** As “a modern authority” he defines “the First Matter is indeed the union of masculine and feminine spirits” [I.2 ¶33; I.2 n34]; it changes form under nature's fire: “The eye of man never saw her twice under one and the same shape” [II.3 ¶30]; he describes it as an eyewitness: “A fat mineral nature it was, he says, bright like pearls, and transparent like crystal” [III.2 n43]. “It is the Light only that can be truly multiplied”, nothing being borrowed from gold or silver [I.2 ¶8]. Atwood says he “has well described” the Hypostatic Metamorphoses: “These three, being but One substantially, admit of a perfect hypostatic union” [III.3 ¶27].

**Method.** Outward study can only “lick the shell” [III.1 ¶8]; theory precedes practice: “be sure to add reason to thy experience, and to employ thy mind as well as thy hands” [III.1 ¶9]; yet “nature is not moved by theory alone, but by sagacious Handicraft and human assistance” [IV.1 ¶5]. Seekers must “change their abstractions into extractions” [II.1 ¶26]. The furnace is small and simple, women fitter than men [III.4 ¶38]; “the excitation of the Fire is a very trivial, slight, almost a ridiculous thing” [III.4 ¶38]; of one heat-operation “whose method is vital and far more mysterious than all other” [IV.1 ¶41]. The second part of the Gross Work is “one of the greatest subtleties of the Art” [IV.1 ¶36]. Further operations are withheld [IV.2 ¶35]; “this dust is the Arabian Elixir” [IV.3 ¶22]. His lessons on self-examination, moderate heat, charity, piety, solitude and perseverance are quoted at length and offered in conclusion of the rest [III.4 ¶44]. He is also cited for uniting the particular spirit to the universal [II.1 ¶26; APP ¶53]; for the triplicity as hidden intrinsical natures, “not of kitchen-stuff, those three pot-principles of water, oil, and earth” [I.3 n30]; for the 'father' of the Seed, “a certain inviolable mass” [II.3 ¶30; II.3 n35]; for uniting heaven and earth in the 'little new world' [II.3 ¶52]; for the garden, “the rendezvous of all spirits, where Ideas as they descend from above, are conceived and incorporated” [II.4 ¶9]; for Hyanthe's tears as the shed Water [III.3 ¶4]; for Agrippa's failure at the second part of the Gross Work [IV.1 ¶36]; and, in *Magia Adamica*, for an early Christian mission to China spreading faith by healing [I.1 ¶26].

**Appendix (later layer).** Every seeker “wanders awhile in the region of Chimaeras” [APP ¶171]; he “very elegantly depicts the play of that ether” [APP ¶105].

E1878.summary: The growth-causing spirit, predominant in the vegetable kingdom.
E1878.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood says: “The Vegetable spirit is the growth-causing spirit” [APP ¶54], predominant in the vegetable kingdom.

E1879.summary: The medium or vehicle of the mind and soul: clear-seeing when purified, terrene when sensual, strengthened by material Rites, and joined by the soul in its ascent.
E1879.body:
Atwood speaks of “the primary and proper vehicle of the mind, when it is in a wise and purified condition, is attenuated and clear seeing” [II.2 ¶15]; when the mind is sensual it is terrene, and unpurified “our vehicle disports herself oftentimes in many mingling forms” [II.2 ¶14]. In the purified ascent “the soul, coalescing with its vehicle, transcends free from corporeal hindrance into the elysian light” [II.4 ¶19].

In II.1 the voice is unclear: the vehicle is what is preserved in nature during the reduction [II.1 ¶47], and “there is no other means of strengthening the vehicle of the sold but by material Rites” [II.1 ¶51].

E1880.summary: In Atwood's reading, Venus personifies the central light of nature, a moist spirit that begets light, liquefies bodies and vivifies metalline bodies.
E1880.body: A passage spoken in Venus's voice: “Now saith Venus: I beget light, nor is the darkness of my nature” [I.3 ¶39]; she liquefies bodies and extracts their substance. Atwood glosses: “Venus personifies the central light of nature” [I.3 n49], a moist spirit vivifying metalline bodies.

E1881.summary: Atwood's name for the true principle of the Divine Art: a divine ray or Power issuing from the will of the divinized.
E1881.body: Atwood states: “This vertical separated Light then we take henceforth to be the true alternative principle in the Divine Art” [III.1 ¶37], a principle about which the alchemists are very wary. It is a divine ray issuing from the will of the divinized: “it is no common light that enters into Divinity, but a congenial ray; a Power” [III.1 ¶37].

E1882.summary: The concealed container in which the Matter is concocted; Atwood calls it internal and a divine secret, and Hermes calls it the philosophers' water.
E1882.body:
Atwood: “the master presupposes not only a knowledge of the Matter, but of the Vessel also in which it is scientifically concocted” [I.3 n22]; a pure vessel contains the ascending waters. She speaks of “that internal fire and vessel of the adepts” [II.1 ¶6], and says the vessel alone is excepted: “with exception of the vessel; which is a divine secret, hidden from idolators” [II.1 ¶8]. Hermes's Latin identifies it: “vas philosophorum est aqua eorum” [II.1 ¶8] (ours: the vessel of the philosophers is their water). She also writes of “this only vessel for its elaboration” [II.1 ¶17]; the context there apparently points to the human circulatory system, but this is an inference.

Norton's *Ordinal* is quoted: “Use one manner of vessel in matter and in shape” [IV.1 ¶28]. At IV.2 three vessels of decreasing opacity are described — “the First indeed may be considered to be opaque, the Second less so, and the Third still less so” — the third holding the one to be born, likened to an embryo's triple covering; in Norton both medicines share one vessel until all quick things are dead, then vessels change [IV.2 ¶11]. Who speaks the three-vessel account is unclear.

E1883.summary: The forecourt before the temple: in man the phantasic intelligence before Reason, in the universe the Ether before the world-soul; mesmerism opens into it.
E1883.body: Atwood's image: what stands before the temple. In man the phantasic intelligence “may be called the vestibule of Reason” [III.1 ¶5]; in the universe the Ether stands before the world-soul [III.1 ¶5]. Mesmerism reaches only this far, “opening into the vestibule” [III.1 ¶8].

E1884.summary: Author of Elements de Psycologie (Paris 1836), cited as having used intuitive certainty to shake the sensual system of Locke and Condillac.
E1884.body: Cited with approval: he used the truth of intuitive certainty to shake the sensual system of Locke and Condillac [II.1 ¶34; II.1 n29].

E1885.summary: Poet whom Atwood reads as an initiate: Aeneid 6 and the Georgics allegorize the Mysteries, the First Matter and the vital transmutation.
E1885.body:
**Initiate and allegorist.** Atwood reads Aeneas's descent in *Aeneid* 6 as an allegory of the Mysteries and holds Virgil initiated: the Sibyl's warning (“Facilis descensus Averni”), the golden bough, cave, reception and “king in hell” [II.3 ¶6–¶19; II.3 n4, n5, n12, n13]. The passage from Tartarus to the Elysian Fields (“Devenere locos laetos, et amoena vireta”) and the Eridanus as a flow of spirit are read as the unfolding of the embryo life [II.4 ¶7; II.4 ¶8; II.4 ¶16; II.4 n3]. Misenus's rites, the hidden tree and Golden Bough (“Hunc tegit omnis Lucus et obscures claudunt convallibus umbrae”) and the mother's birds as guides illustrate the method; she denies he was a servile imitator of Homer [III.1 ¶25–¶35; III.1 n33, n39]. “Spiritus intus alit” illustrates the spirit nourishing heaven, earth and stars [I.2 ¶12; I.2 n14]. His praise of the land (“Salve Magna Parens frugum Saturnia Tellus Magna virum!”) is applied to the vision, though he referred them to his native soul, as the text has it [III.2 ¶27; III.2 ¶28]; “vast, endless, horrible” illustrates the vacuity of the Original of Life [III.2 ¶54]. The site of his Bees, excluding evil associates, figures the right working-place [III.4 ¶42].

**Other.** His death is compared to Vaughan's [I.1 ¶74]; with Ovid, Horace and Vitruvius he was among Augustan men accused of sorcery [I.1 ¶18].

**Appendix (later layer).** Proteus's binding alludes to the First Matter's changing forms; Aristaeus's lost bees are the soul's faculties; the Golden Bough is the aurific seed; the *Georgics* allegorize celestial and spiritual agriculture [APP ¶141; APP ¶144; APP ¶152; APP ¶157]; the Aristaeus myth bears on the Vital transmutation in an advanced stage (“Quis deus hac musae quis nobis extudet artem?”) [APP ¶173].

E1886.summary: In Norton, operative power of four kinds — formal, instrumental, proper and special, material — from which an infused virtue results.
E1886.body: Norton, as quoted, distinguishes four virtues: formal of the orb, instrumental of the eighth sphere, proper and special of the planet, and material of the elements; “The virtue infused resulteth of them all” [IV.2 ¶34].

E1887.summary: Synesius's term, cited by Atwood, for the soul circulating amid her Adamical defilements, which Plato likens to the deformed Glaucus.
E1887.body: Atwood cites the expression from Synesius: “Our viscous soul, as Synesius calls it, circulating in the midst of all her Adamical defilements” [II.3 ¶30]; Plato compares such a soul to the deformed Glaucus [II.3 ¶30].

E1888.summary: The lower visionary stage tied to the co-nascent spirit, whose figured images come from the mind's own fancy.
E1888.body: Atwood describes a lower visionary stage tied to the co-nascent spirit and endured without much disturbing ordinary life; its images are “such as the mind before beheld in Hades from its own self-shadowing creative fancy” [II.4 ¶29].

E1889.summary: The agencies of life which, with their effects, are submitted to subtle analysis and pure synthesis in seeking the Word of Life.
E1889.body: Atwood names the search for the Word of Life a “subtle analysis and pure synthesis of vital agencies and effects” [IV.2 ¶43].

E1890.summary: The adepts' analysis of bodies by which they found man's life to be a pure fire in an ethereal vapour.
E1890.body: Atwood cites “adepts well-skilled, as they profess, in the vital analysis of bodies” [IV.4 ¶4], who by it discovered that man's life is a pure fire in an ethereal vapour; not further explained.

E1891.summary: The impure atmosphere around each individual life, seen by clairvoyants, where thoughts and desires are imaged; purifying it is the Mystery's aim.
E1891.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer), Atwood describes the atmosphere surrounding each individual life, perceived by clairvoyants: “all the thoughts and desires of life are imaged there” [APP ¶73]. Its density or lightness makes men dark or bright, and purifying it is the aim of the Mystery [APP ¶73].

E1892.summary: What the Rational Efficient proceeds to dissolve; not further defined.
E1892.body: Atwood says of the Rational Efficient that “it proceeds even to a dissolution of the Vital Bond” [III.1 ¶47].

E1893.summary: Kirchringius's name for laborious operations amid which the adepts prayed.
E1893.body: Quoted from Kirchringius: “even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed” [III.4 ¶22]. Not further defined.

E1894.summary: Atwood's name for the ancient experimental work on life, the vital alteration of the Mysteries, whose progress discloses powers and secrets of nature.
E1894.body: Atwood's name for the process sketched through the Mysteries in connection with the Sacred Art and Alchemy: “In the progress of this Vital Experiment, it may not be difficult to imagine that powers would be disclosed and particular secrets of nature in the substance of her Whole.” [II.4 ¶58] Part III opens by examining its Method and Principles before the practice: “Let us examine yet further into the Method of this Vital Experiment” [III.1 ¶4].

E1895.summary: The force without which no real transformation occurs; it passes between fermented lives by transmission from agent to patient.
E1895.body: Atwood says no real transformation is achieved “unless the vital force be present and in action” [II.1 ¶5]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, the later layer) it is the life passed between fermented lives, progressing by transmission from agent to patient: “That is the law of progression of the Vital force” [APP ¶42].

E1896.summary: A young discovery, not yet a science, pursued by patiently gathering outward facts.
E1896.body: Atwood: “the discovery of Vital Magnetism is young, and has had no time to grow up into a science” [III.1 ¶8]; it proceeds by gathering outward facts.

E1897.summary: What the purified intelligence dissolves in order to open the occult source.
E1897.body: Atwood says the purified intelligence, “by dissolving the vital medium, opens the occult source” [III.1 ¶23]. Not further defined.

E1898.summary: The perfecting of life, of which the one Art is the medium.
E1898.body: Atwood calls the Art “the one Art and medium of vital perfectibility” [I.1 ¶74], in her praise of Vaughan.

E1899.summary: Principles of life that subsist even in their extreme separation by Art.
E1899.body: Atwood speaks of the “marvelous subsistence of the Vital Principles in their extreme separation by Art” [III.3 ¶9].

E1900.summary: The first stage of the Hermetic Practice, commonly called the Gross Work: purifying the medium of wild affections and defects by dissolution, by the Manual or Linear way.
E1900.body: The heading of IV.1 identifies it: “Of the Vital Purification, Commonly Called the Gross Work” [IV.1 ¶1]. It purifies the medium of its wild affections and innate defects by dissolution; the adepts “proceeded at once scientifically to purify” [IV.1 ¶4], and “for the Purification we read but of one way, called by the Adepts Manual, and their Linear way” [IV.1 ¶5].

E1901.summary: That to which the adepts made experimental ingress, thereby discovering within themselves the catholic original of nature.
E1901.body: Atwood says the adepts, “by an experimental ingress, as they acknowledge, to the Vital Radix, have discovered the catholic original of nature, intellectual and material” [III.2 ¶28].

E1902.summary: Light's greatest and most permanent benefit to man, distinct from its outward use as medicine.
E1902.body: Atwood says Light benefits man as a medicine, “but above all, and most permanently, in the vital rectification” [IV.3 ¶30]. It is not defined, but illustrated by Julian's account of the purified soul strengthening her connate spirit.
